children: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of Rs 1 lakh on Britannia Industries Ltd. for misleading advertisements and unfair trade practices concerning its ‘100% Whole Wheat Bread’ product. The authority has directed the company to discontinue the advertisements with immediate effect and submit a compliance report within 15 days.

In an order dated October 22, 2026, the CCPA held that the prominent ‘100% Whole Wheat Bread’ claim was misleading because the product contained only 62% whole wheat flour, while the remaining 38% comprised other ingredients, including water, yeast, wheat bran and other constituents.

The authority concluded that the claim conveyed the impression that the product consisted entirely of whole wheat flour, contrary to its actual composition. It also held that the accompanying ‘0% Maida’ claim did not cure or mitigate the misleading impression.
CCPA Rejects Britannia’s Defence
The proceedings arose from suo motu cognizance taken by the CCPA over Britannia’s product packaging and advertisements across its website and social media platforms.

Following a preliminary inquiry, the authority issued a notice to the company on January 13, 2025. Britannia submitted its response on January 28, 2025, arguing that the claim referred to the composition of the flour used in the product rather than the composition of the finished bread.

The company maintained that the product contained 62% whole wheat flour and that the remaining ingredients were necessary for manufacturing bread. It also contended that the expression ‘100% Whole Wheat Flour’ was calculated on a flour basis and that the claim was intended to communicate the absence of refined flour or maida.

The CCPA subsequently examined an investigation report dated September 7, 2026, received from the Director General (Investigation), along with findings and observations furnished by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).

According to the order, the FSSAI observed that the use of ‘100%’ in isolation or in conjunction with descriptors could create a false impression of absolute purity or superiority. The investigation also found that the product’s whole wheat flour content was below the prescribed threshold for using the nomenclature ‘Whole Wheat Bread’.
FSSAI Standards And The 75% Threshold

The CCPA referred to Regulation 2.6 of the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Second Amendment Regulations, 2022, which stipulates that whole wheat flour must constitute at least 75% of the prescribed composition for a product to be displayed as ‘Whole Wheat Bread’.

The authority noted that Britannia’s product contained 62% whole wheat flour, below the prescribed threshold. It rejected the company’s argument that the claim should be assessed exclusively on a flour basis, holding that the overall composition and presentation of the finished product were relevant to determining whether consumers were misled.

The order further recorded that the FSSAI had issued an advisory dated May 28, 2025, advising food business operators to discontinue the use of the term ‘100%’ on food product labels, packaging and promotional materials.

The CCPA also noted that, according to the investigation findings, Britannia continued displaying the claim on its website and promotional channels despite the advisory and subsequent regulatory communications.
CCPA Finds Disclaimer Insufficient

The authority observed that the product’s front packaging prominently displayed ‘100% Whole Wheat Bread’, alongside the ‘0% Maida’ claim. A qualifying statement on the reverse side read: ‘Made from 100% Whole Wheat Flour on Flour Basis’.

The CCPA held that the disclaimer, linked to the front-label claim through a symbol and presented in comparatively small print, did not adequately correct the impression created by the prominent claim.

It observed that an ordinary consumer might not examine the detailed ingredient declaration before purchasing the product. The authority also found that the placement and presentation of the qualification made it insufficiently prominent to clarify the actual composition.

The CCPA further considered the accompanying representation that the bread ‘pairs perfectly well with a healthy diet’, holding that the overall packaging could create an impression about the product’s dietary suitability that was not adequately substantiated by its composition.
Findings Under The Consumer Protection Act, 2019

The CCPA held that the representations violated Section 2(28) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which defines misleading advertisements, and constituted an unfair trade practice under Section 2(47).
The authority also referred to Section 2(9), concerning consumer rights, including the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods.

In addition, the order referred to Regulation 4(1) of the Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018, and the Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements, 2022.

The CCPA concluded that the prominent numerical claim, combined with the limited prominence of the qualifying disclosure, misrepresented the product’s composition and could influence consumers’ purchasing decisions.
Exercising its powers under Sections 10, 18, 20 and 21 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the CCPA issued the following directions to Britannia Industries Ltd.:
1. Discontinuation of advertisements: Immediately discontinue the false and misleading advertisements across print and electronic media, including social media.
2. Monetary penalty: Pay a penalty of Rs 1,00,000 for engaging in misleading advertisements and unfair trade practices.
3. Compliance report: Submit a report to the CCPA on compliance with the directions within 15 days from the date of the order.

The order reinforces the CCPA’s position that food-product claims must be assessed in the context of the product’s actual composition and the overall impression conveyed to an ordinary consumer. It also underscores that a qualifying statement in fine print may not be sufficient to neutralise a prominent, potentially misleading claim on product packaging.
